content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has released the third edition of its consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis, focusing on rapid diagnostic methods for TB detection. This updated publication builds upon the second edition, which was released in 2021, and incorporates the latest advancements in diagnostic technologies and methodologies. The guidelines are available in both electronic and print formats, with respective ISBNs 978-92-4-008948-8 and 978-92-4-008949-5. The publication is protected under a Creative Commons license, allowing for non-commercial use, adaptation, and redistribution, provided proper citation is given. However, the WHO logo cannot be used, and any adaptations must be licensed under equivalent terms. The guidelines emphasize the importance of rapid diagnostic tests, including nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), line probe assays (LPAs), and next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies, for detecting TB and drug-resistant TB. These methods are evaluated for their diagnostic accuracy, feasibility, and cost-effectiveness. The document also includes systematic reviews and meta-analyses of various diagnostic tools, such as Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra, for detecting TB in adults, children, and individuals with extrapulmonary TB or HIV. The development of these guidelines involved extensive collaboration among experts from diverse fields, including members of the WHO Global TB Programme, regional offices, and external review groups. The guideline development process adhered to rigorous methodologies, including conflict-of-interest assessments and systematic reviews of diagnostic accuracy, economic evidence, and user perspectives. The WHO acknowledges the contributions of numerous professionals, organizations, and funding agencies, including USAID and Unitaid, while maintaining that the content of the guidelines was not influenced by the views of these funding bodies. The guidelines also provide detailed recommendations on the use of low-complexity automated NAATs, high-complexity reverse hybridization-based NAATs, and targeted NGS for detecting resistance to firstand second-line anti-TB drugs. Additionally, they address the diagnostic performance of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) and lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) assays, particularly for individuals living with HIV. The publication includes annexes detailing the guideline development methods, conflict-of-interest assessments, and the composition of the guideline development and external review groups. It also features systematic reviews on the diagnostic accuracy and economic evaluations of molecular assays, as well as qualitative research on user perspectives and feasibility. Overall, the WHO consolidated guidelines aim to provide evidence-based recommendations to improve TB diagnosis and management globally, with a focus on ensuring accessibility, accuracy, and cost-effectiveness of diagnostic tools in diverse healthcare settings.
